chapter: Safe streets, decline and club life at San Jacinto
title: Safe streets in the 1930s and walking home from gigs
summary: Harold and Mitchell contrast safe nights then with today, recalling walking home with a horn and cheap sandwiches.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Oh. Like, like, could you say in the, in the thirties and forties, could you just walk around the streets at night and nobody would bother you or anything?
That's right. I used to walk.
You could sleep with your doors open and things, didn't I?

I used to walk on the roof garden sometime, you know, I used to walk on the roof garden, I used to walk on the back, and then I used to sit there and then I lived back on the man's street, I'd walk from the roof garden. In other words, when we played at Charlie Armstead down there in the night one, we had to walk to St. Claude Street to get a street car if the Claiborne car stopped at twelve o'clock. See, we'd walk to St. Claude Street.
Yeah. You couldn't do that now.
No, you wouldn't have your horn when you get to that. Right.
Yeah, you're bred of his own.
Yeah. That's rough. I just wondered, because you know now everybody's scared to go out. Yeah. Out too much, or out of their neighborhood.

Yeah, but it was nice before you, I mean you could walk, like I used to come from, when I lived on the mania of prayer, I used to come from the Popeye every night around 1929, 30 like that. I used to walk from the Gator Street like that, stop at Joe Sheep and get a, about ten of them
and get a dine sandwiches and that. I mean.
Stuffed sweet pepper, hot-sized pork chop, anything you wanted. Anything you wanted. A dime would stay in the saddle. Oh boy. You couldn't get away with that now.
